title: Postgres slow-query profiler CLI
subtitle: Real-word .com domains are gone. Move to .dev, or buy one on the aftermarket.
domain_mode: B. Free on .com or on a developer TLD

brief.does: Reads your Postgres slow-query log and names the index you are missing
brief.audience: Backend engineers. They type it several times a day.
brief.positioning: A precision instrument, not a platform. It does one job with no agent and no dashboard.
brief.personality: Technical and precise. Unfashionable on purpose.
brief.constraints: Short and easy to type. One word under 8 characters. npm and PyPI should be free for later installers.

assumptions: Go binary, installed through a Homebrew tap
No commercial launch yet, so trademark and app stores are out of scope

territories.name: Depth sounding
territories.description: The instruments sailors used to find the bottom before sonar. A weighted line dropped into water you cannot see through.
territories.fit: The tool finds the expensive thing hidden inside a system you have no view into. The metaphor maps almost exactly.

territories.name: Diagnostics
territories.description: Vitals, triage, symptoms, the patient chart.
territories.fit: It fits the job. Every observability tool is already here, so the names sound like the category rather than like you.

territories.name: Divining
territories.description: Finding water underground by reading what shows on the surface.
territories.fit: The mechanism is right and the words are unused. It fights the precision positioning. See the Dowse weakness.

territories.name: Craft and sharpening
territories.description: Whetstone, hone, grindstone. The tools that keep other tools working.
territories.fit: It fits the promise of making a slow thing fast. Developer tooling has used these words heavily.

territories.name: Cartography
territories.description: Atlas, contour, seam. The query plan read as terrain.
territories.fit: Accurate but abstract. The names come out sounding like generic data tooling.

rounds.focus: Six to ten names in each of the five territories, checked on .com and .dev
rounds.note: 1 free on **.com** against 14 on **.dev**. Two-word compounds of common English words were registered between 1995 and 2010. This settles the TLD, not the name.
Same rate. The territory is healthy. The .com problem is not about these words.

rounds.focus: The strongest stems as short command-shaped words, adding .sh
rounds.note: Single real words are gone on .com. Most are free on .dev and .sh.

candidates.name: Sounder
candidates.why: A sounder is the instrument that measures depth. Engineers read the word correctly the first time, with nothing to explain. It types cleanly as a command: `sounder analyze`.
candidates.weakness: Sounder is also a bird and a piece of audio equipment. Read cold it can land as a comparative adjective, as in "sounder judgment". PyPI already holds the name.

clearance.detail: searched the name alone, not the name plus postgres

searchability.note: Shares the term with a seabird and with audio hardware. Adding "postgres" to the query clears it, so expect to lose the bare term for the first year.

candidates.name: Leadsman
candidates.why: The leadsman drops the weighted line and calls out the depth. He is not the navigator. He reports what is under you. That is this tool's job. Two syllables that spell themselves. No other developer tool uses the word.
candidates.weakness: You have to know the word for the name to mean anything. Anyone who does not will hear "lead" as a sales lead first.
candidates.verdict: Take it if your users enjoy a name that rewards knowing something.

searchability.note: Almost nothing else uses the word. You would be the first result within weeks.

candidates.name: Dowse
candidates.why: Five letters and one syllable. Free on both developer TLDs. To dowse is to find what is underground by reading the surface. That is what the tool does to a query plan.
candidates.weakness: Dowsing is pseudoscience. This tool sells precision. Naming it after the best-known unscientific method is a real conflict. Some engineers will read it as a joke.
candidates.verdict: Best shape of the three. Only works if the reference reads as confident.

searchability.note: Dowsing has a large existing body of results. The developer sense would have to be built.

candidates.name: By the Mark
candidates.why: The leadsman's actual call. "By the mark, twain" is the depth read off the knots in the line. The name points at the reading rather than at the person taking it, which is what a reporting tool produces.
candidates.weakness: Three words. As a binary it collapses to `bythemark` or `btm`. Neither is good to type.
candidates.verdict: Highest ceiling in the run. Wrong shape for a command line.

searchability.note: A phrase nobody else claims. Long-tail queries land on you immediately.

candidates.name: Plumbline
candidates.why: A weight on a string that finds true vertical. People who have never been near a boat still know the word, so it costs no explanation.
candidates.weakness: Nine characters with two stressed syllables. It types and speaks heavier than the rest. Both .com and .dev are taken, so there is no clean domain.
candidates.verdict: Better word than Leadsman. No route to a domain.

searchability.note: A common term in construction and in scripture. You would not own this.

candidates.name: Slipstream
candidates.why: The low-drag pocket behind a moving object. Anyone understands it with no background.
candidates.weakness: Used as a product name across several industries. It describes the result rather than the method, so it would suit any performance tool equally well.
candidates.verdict: Aftermarket only. Not worth BrandBucket pricing.

searchability.note: Used as a product name across several industries. The term is not winnable.

candidates.name: Deadreckon
candidates.why: Dead reckoning estimates your position from speed and heading when you cannot see land. Query planning works the same way.
candidates.weakness: "Dead" in the name of a database tool suggests downtime. That association is free and unwanted.
candidates.verdict: Wrong tone. Resolve the failed lookup before spending more time on it.

searchability.note: Dead reckoning is a well-documented navigation method. The one-word spelling helps a little.

top3.name: Sounder
top3.reason: It types well and reads correctly cold. Nothing needs explaining.
top3.dealbreaker: PyPI already holds the name, so a Python installer would ship as `sounder-cli`.

top3.name: Leadsman
top3.reason: The better metaphor. The worse first impression.
top3.dealbreaker: Too many of your users will hear "sales lead".

top3.name: Dowse
top3.reason: The best-shaped word here, free on both developer TLDs.
top3.dealbreaker: You have to defend "precision tooling" against a name meaning pseudoscience.

unconventional.name: By the Mark
unconventional.reason: Phrase names are rare in developer tooling, so people remember them.
unconventional.cost: You lose the clean binary name.

safest.name: Sounder
safest.reason: Register `sounder.dev`, publish npm as `sounder` and PyPI as `sounder-cli`.

unverified: Search covered the names alone, not the name plus postgres. A collision inside the category could still exist. Check before you announce.
`deadreckon.dev` returned HTTP 429 after four attempts. That is **unresolved. It is not available.**
No trademark search was run. That is fine for a hobby CLI. It stops being fine the day you charge for it.
A GitHub result of `taken` means the org exists. Several of these are dormant accounts. GitHub rarely releases them.
Social handles were not checked. Platform status codes are wrong in both directions often enough to be useless. Open the signup pages yourself.
